To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
orthologues are more likely to share function, to share the same subcellular location, and to be co-expressed than paralogues.
orthologous genes are not always equivalent, orthologous gene pairs are not always conserved and paralogous genes are not all equivalent.

(1) orthologous genes tend to be functionally related, (2) paralogous genes often share functions, (3) orthologous and paralogous genes tend to have similar expression patterns, and (4) the functional similarity of orthologous and/or paralogous genes is often associated with similar evolutionary rates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolutionary implications of gene duplication, the functional consequences of gene loss, the evolution of gene expression and the evolutionary conservation of gene regulatory networks.

the evolution and function of genes and their products, and how this relates to the evolution and function at the level of the organism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
orthology is not a sufficient condition for functional equivalence but is a necessary condition, whereas paralogy is not a sufficient nor a necessary condition for functional divergence.
orthologous genes tend to retain their original function in the new species, but that this is not always the case.
orthology is a useful concept, but that its application to the study of gene–phenotope relationships requires caution and care.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the orthology–paralogy distinction, although useful, is not as clear-cut as often assumed and should be used with caution.
orthology and paralogues do not necessarily imply functional conservation and divergence, respectively.
the functional implications of orthology are not as clear as we might hope, and that the evolutionary consequences are more complex than previously assumed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
orthologues and paralogs do not necessarily share key properties.
orthologues do not always retain the same function in different organisms.
orthology is not a binary concept and that the functional and evolutionary implications of orthology are not always straightforward.
